I do not think that a 14 factual elaboration along the same lines will help your Honours 15 much further. In our motion we have set out in detail and per 17 allegation the contradictory and flawed evidence that has 18 undermined the claim of the Prosecution that all charges will be 19 proved beyond reasonable doubt. Where witnesses gave 20 conflicting accounts, false allegations or tenuous 21 identifications, we have shown that there is no case to answer. Here I would like to cite Cross and Tapper On 23 Evidence, edition 1995 at page 192, where they write: "Questions of the sufficiency of evidence are usually 25 raised on a submission that there is no case to answer. The 26 Judge must rule in favour of the submission if there is 27 insufficient evidence to prove an essential element in the ... 28 case, or if the evidence which has been adducted is so tenuous that no jury properly directed could convict upon it. It is not enough when any weakness in the ... case depends on matters within the exclusive jurisdiction of the jury, such as reliability of witnesses." They also write: "While honesty of a witness should properly remain to be decided by the jury, there are situations, such as identification, where the evidence even of an honest witness might be regarded as tenuous." Another issue ---- 10 JUDGE STEPHEN: Could you repeat the page in Cross and Tapper? 11 MR. WLADIMIROFF: That is page 192. 12 JUDGE STEPHEN: Thank you. 13 MR. WLADIMIROFF: Your Honour, another issue I would like to elaborate a little bit further is the requirement of corroboration of evidence. Different to common law jurisdictions where one witness is sufficient in all cases, most civil law jurisdictions maintain the unus testis nullus testis rule. Bearing this in mind, it seems significant to me that Rule 96(i) states expresses verbis that "no corroboration of the victim's testimony shall be required" in the context of a rape case. This requirement would not make any sense if corroboration of evidence would not be required at all. A reasonable interpretation a contrario, therefore, is that in other cases the corroboration is indeed required. This interpretation is consistent with Rule 89(B) that stipulates that a Chamber shall apply rules of evidence which will best 28 1 favour a fair examination of matters before it and are 2 consonant with the spirit of the Statute and the general 3 principles of law. In this connection, I would like to mention that the 5 Court heard evidence from one witness only on counts 12, 13 and 6 14. Talking about the spirit of the Statute and general 8 principles of law, I emphasise that a fundamental tenet of civil 9 law jurisdictions is that in order to amount to corroboration, 10 the evidence has to emanate from a source independent of the 11 witness to be corroborated or, in a still extreme form, from a 12 different type of source from the witness to be corroborated. More in general I note that where the indictment 14 contains a number of similar counts reflecting a succession of 15 different incidents related by common factors, of course each 16 count will have to be considered separately. Citing Cross and Tapper again at page 168 up to 169, 18 I may reflect the opinion of the Court of south Australia in the 19 R. v. Van Beelen case responding to the question if there can be 20 satisfaction beyond reasonable doubt of guilt of the accused 21 when there is no such satisfaction with regard to any of the 22 evidentiary facts. On this, the Court expressed itself as 23 follows: "There is a clear distinction between drawing an 25 inference of guilt from a combination of several proved acts, 26 none of which by itself would support the inference, and drawing 27 an inference of guilt from several facts whose existence is in 28 1 doubt. In the first place, the combination does what each fact 2 taken in isolation could not do; in the second case the 3 combination counts for nothing. " Finally, I would like to recall that Article 7 of the 5 Statute holds a person responsible, who planned, instigated, 6 committed or otherwise aided and abetted in the planning, 7 preparation or execution of a crime. The Defence takes the position that participation 10 within the criminal responsibility of the Statute requires an 11 active involvement in the execution of a crime. It is not 12 enough to be present whilst a crime is committed, if the accused 13 takes no part in it and does not act in concert with those who 14 commit it, unless he watched for his companions in order to 15 permit the commission of the crime. The evidence does not meet 16 this standard. If I may conclude my arguments, your Honours? The 18 removal of allegations not proven, and the stigma attached, at 19 the earliest possible opportunity is a prime objective of any 20 criminal justice system. The deliberate retention (as the 21 Prosecution wishes) of unsubstantiated allegations that may be 22 removed at an appropriate stage would be a clear breach of 23 Article 7 of the International Covenant, which provision, 24 although not strictly binding, should guide the Trial Chamber in 25 this matter. We trust that the Trial Chamber will find that the 27 allegations as discussed in our motion are indeed 28 unsubstantiated. We request you to dismiss these counts against Dusko Tadic. utterances.text: As a practical matter, it is likely to work that way in a state 27 where you have a pronounced majority narod. Your problems come 28 in the portions of states where, for example, one of the minorities is a local majority and say, "We are a narod, we have the right to secede", or in Bosnia and Herzegovina where there is no majority narod and where, for example, where the Croats of western Herzegovina, for example, proclaimed their own mini state within Bosnia and Herzegovina on the grounds of the right to self-determination and self-determination of the narod, which is the constitutional structure. 9 JUDGE STEPHEN: I thought that in those excerpts from most, but not all because Bosnia-Herzegovina was not included, of the republics there was a careful inclusion in the statement of who the people were, not only of the majority narod but also of others that was recognised, and they were recognised as being citizens, were they not? 15 A. Citizens but not part of the sovereign body which is -- well, it is not a state of equal citizens. There may be citizens of the state, but they are not part of the sovereign body. If one reads the speeches and the position and papers of the various political leaders, they are very clear about this. This is not a type of structure that we are used to thinking about, because we would like to posit a polity of equal citizens. This is the modern meaning of democracy. Here, though, only one part of the citizenry is sovereign. 24 Q. Although that does not in fact emerge, does it, from those small portions that you quote? You have to look at what the leaders say? 27 A. This is true. I find the formulation, though, in the preambles 28 of the constitution to be extremely indicative of what it is all about and then prefer Dr. Tudjman's speech to actually state the point perhaps more clearly than I have. I might draw a rather different parallel. The point of the socialist state was to serve, to represent, not the entire population, but only part of the population, the working class and the working people, which is what the state is there for constitutionally defined, legally implemented. What succeeded state socialism in the former Yugoslav Republics was another form of a state in which the state is there, constitutionally defined and legally implemented, to serve one part of the population and that is the majority narod. 13 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: As you said, if we had a constitution which said, "We, the white Protestant", cross out even males ---- 15 THE WITNESS: Could be that as well. 16 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: "in order to form a more perfect union." 17 THE WITNESS: Yes. 18 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Then you go on to mention some other people, you wonder who are the narods? 20 THE WITNESS: Particularly when the amendment is made from the all-inclusive "we, the people" and then suddenly amendments are inserted that say, "We, the white Protestant male people and others.". 24 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Orie, you say you have listed this witness for two days and if this continues -- so we will be quiet. I will be quiet. 27 MR. ORIE: I think we will manage, your Honour. I am still 28 optimistic that we will manage. 2 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: We have heard so much testimony. Obviously, as we have said, we have read through these transcripts and we are now at the point of trying to resolve in our minds some questions. One of them had to do with ethnicity. Unfortunately, Professor Hayden, you came ---- 7 MR. ORIE: Your Honour, I will tell you that I will not cover in the testimony of Dr. Hayden questions concerning all the issues dealt with by Dr. Gow. So we will concentrate on certain issues. 11 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: OK. 12 MR. ORIE: Professor Hayden, could you please have a look at Exhibit 21 that is presented to you, as I understand? 14 A. Yes, I am holding it. 15 Q. Could you just tell us what you understand it is? 16 A. Well, it is a photocopy of the memorandum, the famous memorandum, of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts of 1986. It is from the Zagreb magazine Nase Teme from 1989 and it has attached a translation, it has attached an English translation. 21 Q. Dr. Gow has testified on this memorandum. Could you please tell us whether this memorandum was unique to Serbia, such a document? 24 A. The memorandum discusses the problems of the Serbs in Yugoslavia, and as a document discussing the problems of one of the nations of Yugoslavia the memorandum was certainly not unique at the time that it was written and not published. It 28 was never adopted by the Serbian Academy, and in fact it was not published until it was pirated into a Zagreb magazine, a Croatian magazine in 1989, but it was by no means the only such document in Yugoslavia in the late 80s. 5 Q. If you say it was not the only document, this memorandum, could you point to similar documents that have been prepared and discussed elsewhere within the federation? 8 A. The primary document that I would think of would be something called the Slovenian National Programme which was a set of articles drafted by Slovenian intellectuals in approximately 1986/87, in other words at the same time that the group of -- they were literally identified on the cover as a group of intellectuals of the Serbian Academy. The Slovenian National Programme was published in Slovenia in a journal called Nova Revija, New Review, in 1987. 16 Q. Could you tell us have you ever seen that document, the Slovenian National Programme? 18 A. I have seen the document, yes, I have held the document, yes, when I was in Slovenia in 1989. It was a magazine that had been openly for sale. 21 Q. It was published? 22 A. Oh, yes, it was published in the magazine Nova Revija, New Review, which was a magazine which I think itself came into existence in the 1980s in Slovenia and was, essentially, the magazine of Slovenian nationalist intellectuals. 26 Q. Professor Hayden, did you obtain a copy of the document? 27 A. No. At the time when I was in Slovenia in 1989 I saw it at a 28 friend's home. My friend had it. I could see it, but I was not able to acquire a copy then. I have to say I did not, it did not occur to me, well, it occurred to me but making a copy then of the entire journal, I figured I would get it elsewhere. Making photocopies in Yugoslavia at that time was expensive and I thought I would get it, but I never did. 7 Q. I would like to present to you another document, Professor Hayden, because I would like to ask you some questions on whether this document really existed. 10 A. This is a photocopy of actually two articles that appeared in consecutive issues of a weekly newspaper in Belgrade called Nedeljni Telegraph or Weekly Telegraph, the issue of 24th July 1996, the issue of 31 July 1996. It is an article about a meeting between Serbian intellectuals and Slovenian intellectuals in 1985. 16 Q. Could you please -- unfortunately, your Honour, we have not been able to have a translation made of this document. First I tender this document as an Exhibit. 19 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: That will be 46? 20 MR. ORIE: That will be 46, your Honour, yes. 21 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Any objection? It is only in Serbo-Croatian? 22 THE WITNESS: Yes. 23 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Are you asking the witness to read a portion of it? 25 MR. ORIE: Yes. I will ask the witness to read portions of it. The main reason why I am doing this is since we cannot present, as you have heard, Slovenian National Programme, I would like to 28 establish that this document did exist and some support of the memory of Professor Hayden as to the existence and the content of the document he saw at that time. 4 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Niemann, any objection? 5 MR. NIEMANN: No, your Honour. 6 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Very good, 46 will be admitted. 7 THE WITNESS: Perhaps I should say that I had first heard of the meeting of Serbian intellectuals and Slovene intellectuals that is reported in this document from Professor Markotic who is listed as author and whose picture is on the front page. I heard about this from him in a conversation that I had with him in January 1991 in Belgrade five years ago and six years after the event. 14 MR. ORIE: Yes. Would you please point at the relevant parts of this article, and perhaps read slowly those parts that are referring to this movement, this meeting, and this Slovenian National Programme? 18 A. Was this given to the translators as well? 19 Q. We have given the relevant parts to the translators in order to facilitate a quick translation. 21 A. Well, what I would like to do is read several passages from here. I prepared myself a photocopy in which I marked the passages so that I could find them easily. I believe that a similar copy was given to the translators so that they would be able to follow it. 26 Q. If you could perhaps also indicate those parts on the overhead projector where the original Exhibit is. 28 1 A. Right. Starting here with the words Slovenci, and I am afraid the translators will have to put up with my accent in Serbo-Croatian, but then you will listen to the translation instead of me and you will be better off. For the translators this would be the excerpt marked No. 1 on the copy they have. [In translation] "Today the Slovenians feel that the idea of belonging of Slovenes in Yugoslavia is dead or if nothing else dying. People feel disappointed and disillusioned and deceived in their expectations. We have nothing to expect any longer. We do not feel that we are in our own country. As a state product Yugoslavia is dead in the minds of the people." The speaker is Bucar, later the President of the Slovenian National Assembly. If we go further down the page, and there is no real easy way to do this. 17 Q. Perhaps you could get some help. 18 A. Do I have to show it on the screen as well as read it? 19 Q. I think perhaps it is easier, especially since Dr. Gow is there, if you indicate what part you are reading. 21 A. OK. The speaker is still Bucar and where my finger is -- yes, beginning with the words -- the pointer is on it. Can you get it over to there. I see it but I do not see the pointer. 24 Q. You should perhaps move the document a bit so that the pointer is in the picture as well. 26 A. It is right here beginning with the word "Yesu" which is still not on here. 28 1 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: If you put your highlighted copy on the overhead and then turn, if they will turn that towards you, Mr. Usher, see if you can turn it over. 4 THE WITNESS: We want passage No. 2. 5 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: You can turn the elmo towards the witness. 6 THE WITNESS: OK. It is the point marked No. 2 and outlined and highlighted in pink. Again I think the speaker is Bucar. [ In translation] "Are the Serbs nationalists? If they are, good for them. Unfortunately, there is a major difference between the Slovenians and Serbs as nationalists. To our mind, the idea of Yugoslav-hood is of secondary importance. To you it is of primary importance. We want autonomy and for you Yugoslavia has been and still is the road to the solution of the Serb question. What interest could we have in common then?" No. 3, the speaker here is Yanez Urbancic with whom I am not actually familiar. [In translation] "The fundamental thing for me is that I am a Slovene, that I love my people and my language, and I want to remain that. I have no visions about future Yugoslavia. The most important thing is that this fundamental national identity of mine ought to be inviolate and respected in it." From the second article -- no, I missed one. Again, I am sorry, we have not had these translated. The Translation Service was not able to do this. I would like to see four. I believe the speaker is still Urbancic. This is again No. 4. [In translation] "Nevertheless, the principal 28 1 contradiction between the view that the people with a fatherland 2 is the vital thing and the universalists or even Marxist theory 3 that there are more important things from the national 4 determination. A whole movement has two meanings. On the one 5 hand, integration of Europe includes universalism. On the 6 other, on the opposite side is the movement for the 7 manifestation of national rights. Nonetheless, the people 8 cannot be a tool of anything else, socialism, communism. A 9 people is a means, a purpose unto itself." From the second article 31 July, the speaker here is Tone 11 Hribar who, as I recall, was editor of Nova Revija. Perhaps 12 I should explain here because he makes a reference to something 13 called the Yavnosti. Yavnost was supposed to be a magazine in 14 Serbia that was going to be begun by opposition intellectuals, 15 opposition to the regime, the Communist regime, and it was not 16 in fact begun. The state did not permit it to exist, but the 17 comparison here is between Nova Revija, the Slovenian journal, 18 and Yavnosti, the Serbian one that was going to be initiated by 19 the Serbian participants in this discussion. [In translation] "I need to say that the initiative to 21 start Nova Revija was started here as early as 1980, slightly 22 before Yavnost. Yavnost attempted to be a Yugoslav journal and 23 we thought that it ought first to assert itself as a Serb 24 journal and then the integration could come about." Just a couple more, if you will bear with me. The speaker 26 in No. 5 is Taras Kermaner who was and is a Slovenian writer. [In translation] "How different it is with Serbs for 28 1 whom Yugoslav is an objective interest and need because they are 2 torn and discordant. If Yugoslavia were to break apart Serbs 3 would lose almost half of the population." This is Yugoslavia 4 in World War II (?) [In translation] "Avner (?) Yugoslavia promoted 6 brotherhood and unity which was a substitute for the autonomy 7 and civil society, but brotherhood always means terror and 8 demagogy and unity means homogenization". I should add that "Bretsvo Jedicstvo" brotherhood and 10 unity, was one of the primary ideological bases of the 11 Yugoslavia that existed under Tito and until 1991. The 12 constitution of 1974 makes fairly frequent references to Bretsvo 13 Jedicstvo, brotherhood and unity. Finally, the speaker is again France Bucar. [In translation] "The Serbs need to follow their own 16 national interest. We are for confederalism. However, the 17 solution to the problem is not within the categories of 18 federalism or confederalism. I respect your nationalism but it 19 comes into conflict with the Slovenian national concept." Thank you. As I said, these intellectuals, among others, 21 wrote a Slovenian national programme that was published in Nova 22 Revija in 1987, as it indicates here. Bucar had a certain 23 political success in Slovenia later. I can say that other 24 contributors to Nova Revija also had political success in the 25 elections in 1990 in the victory of the nationalist coalition 26 that won then and has governed the governments of Slovenia since 27 1990. 28 1 Q. Professor Heyden, do I understand well that this political language was used far before the memorandum was drafted, the memorandum which was Exhibit 21? 4 A. Yes, this meeting took place in 1985 and the memorandum was written or begun in 1986. I also remember that one of the people whose words I read here, Taras Kermaner, had quite shocked the Serbian intellectual public in I think it was the summer of 1985 or 1986 with a so-called "letter to my Serbian friend" first published in Slovenia and then republished in Serbia. That was very much of an anti-Yugoslav polemic and in many ways an anti-Serbian one as well. 12 Q. Professor Hayden, I would like you to be shown now Prosecution Exhibit 24. 14 JUDGE STEPHEN: I think I should say that I do not follow at all what all this comes to. Perhaps I am not intended to at this stage, but to me it is meaningless the last 20 minutes. 17 MR. ORIE: Your Honour, I will try to explain to you what it is all about. A lot of attention has been paid by the Prosecutor to sovereignty, the right to secession, where it all started. What the Defence intends to do is to give a different picture, first of all, to clarify a few constitutional issues, then to make clear that the statement of Dr. Gow, that it all started -- and that is one of my next questions -- were compared and the conclusions drawn by Dr. Gow, especially from Exhibit 24, confront this witness with it and see if he comes to the same conclusion, the main conclusion of Dr. Gow being that this nationalistic movement mainly arose in Serbia, in the Belgrade 28 areas, and to see whether this is also the opinion of Professor Hayden. The relevance of it I think stems from the relevance attached to it by the Prosecution. That is the reason why we do not want to have it unanswered, and the relevance for the whole case of course still has to be considered later on. Professor Hayden, Exhibit 24, could you please bring into our mind what Exhibit 24 is? 8 A. 24 is an English translation of the constitution of the Republic of Serbia from 1990. 10 Q. I would like to take you to a part which, as I understand, is not exactly the text of the constitution itself, on pages 10, 11, small numbers, which is a part written, as far as I understand, by a certain Mr. Markotich. 14 A. Yes. 15 Q. Could you please give your comment on that part, the last part? 16 A. Referring to the last paragraph? 17 Q. Yes. 18 A. It says: "Due to the present constitutional status of Serbia, the question may arise as to whether Serbia with the new constitution has turned its back to the Federal Yugoslavia. By the new constitution Serbia has only made more precise the character of its link with Yugoslavia. Serbia has entirely recognised the primacy of the federal constitution until Yugoslavia continues to have the federal order." I suspect the translation is wrong and it should have said, "while Yugoslavia continues to have a federal order". "Some other non-Federal Yugoslavia is beyond the political and state interest of Serbia 28 precisely because of that and due to the tendency of squandering the Federal Yugoslavia" which is now visible "Serbia had to include in its constitution the 'defensive clause' to a violation of the federal constitution that the detriment of Serbia entitles Serbia to self-defence in such cases, namely, republic authorities shall issue acts in order to protect the interests of the Republic of Serbia." 8 Q. Professor Hayden, this constitution has been used as I think the basis for the opinion of Dr. Gow that this was an illustration, it was showing that Serbia was preparing for the dissolution of Yugoslavia. Would you agree with that opinion of Dr. Gow? 12 A. I am not sure what he meant by preparing for the dissolution of Yugoslavia. It certainly comes up in the context in which the constitutional order of Yugoslavia has been threatened, but not in this particular set of concerns by Serbia. 16 Q. So it was not Serbia but the other republics? 17 A. Specifically Slovenia. 18 Q. Specifically Slovenia. May I draw your attention perhaps because it might be one of the relevant articles of this constitution, Article 135 of that constitution contained in Exhibit 24. 22 A. OK. It is Chapter 8 the relationship to the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. 24 Q. Could you please tell us what the first paragraph of Article 135 is about? 26 A. Actually I cannot. As printed it does not make sense. 27 Q. Could you please -- it is on the screen. So you do not 28 understand it? 2 A. No, this sentence is meaningless to me, "The rights and duties vested under the present constitution in the Republic of Serbia which is part of the socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, violate the equal terms of the federal constitution are to be exercised in the federation." Grammatically it is wrong. It does not scan. 8 Q. Could I then please provide you with the original text of Article 135. I tender the original text as an Exhibit, your Honour. 11 A. OK, yes, this is a photocopy of the constitution of the Republic of Serbia in Serbian, dated Belgrade 1990, and Article 135. 13 Q. Then I would like to present to you a text which is supposed to be a translation of Article 135. 15 A. Actually, I have to get the original back. 16 MR. ORIE: I tender this document as well, your Honour, as Exhibit 47. 18 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Any objection? 19 MR. NIEMANN: No, your Honour. 20 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Exhibit 47 will be admitted. 21 MR. ORIE: I would like to have ---- 22 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Excuse me one minute, Mr. Orie. I was just thinking, Mr. Orie, I gather where you are going is that this witness, whoever translated it, will offer a different translation than what we received from the Prosecutor in Exhibit 24 for Article 135 which we will, if there is no objection, receive that. But we have encountered so many difficulties with 28 interpretation -- not so many but some -- we, perhaps, would want the Serbo-Croatian then to be put on the screen after we see this and have our interpreters translate it and then see among the three what we come up with. 5 MR. ORIE: Yes. You see, your Honour, there was no attention paid to Article 135 in the Prosecution's case, so that is the reason why we did not notice at that moment that on this part, in our view, the translation was incorrect. But I have some difficulties asking Professor Hayden questions about a part of an article that is totally un-understandable for him. 11 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: I understand your point and 47 is admitted. Let us see what his translation is. I suppose I am just curious, if it does not take too much time, to see what we might get as a third. So here it is. 15 THE WITNESS: Well, clause 1: "The rights and duties that the Republic of Serbia which is within the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia has under this constitution and which by the federal constitution are realised within the federation will be realised in accordance with the federal constitution." 20 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Is that the ---- 21 THE WITNESS: That is clause 1, this is in Serbian. 22 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: That is Serbo -- that is in Serbian? Excuse me. 24 THE WITNESS: Well, I speak Serbo-Croatian but ...... 25 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: It is there. I do not know that the interpreters have it. Can you read it well enough to interpret it? OK. Let us see. This is now the interpreters' translation 28 of Article 135 of Prosecutor's Exhibit 24 and we have the English translation in Defence Exhibit 47. 3 THE INTERPRETER: "The rights and duties of the Republic of Serbia being a part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia enjoys under this constitution, and which are to be exercised at a federal level under the or according to the federal constitution shall be exercised" ----- 8 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Do we have the channel 4? 9 THE WITNESS: I did not. I now do. 10 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: If you could begin again, please? 11 THE INTERPRETER: "The rights and duties which the Republic of Serbia being a part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia enjoys under this constitution and which pursuant to the federal constitution are exercised or enjoyed at the federal level, rather, in the federation, at the federal level, shall be exercised in conformity or in accordance with the federal constitution. "When acts of federal agencies or acts of agencies of another Republic in contravention to the rights and duties which that Republic which it has, which that Republic enjoys under the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia violate or infringe upon the quality of the Republic of Serbia", and we cannot see the rest of the text -- "infringe upon", whatever, "rights of the Republic of Serbia" -- I am sorry, I have forgotten -- "or threatens its interests, or infringes upon its interests in any other way without providing a compensation or indemnity for it, then the Republican agencies shall adopt 28 acts to protect the interests of the Republic of Serbia." 2 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Thank you very much. 3 MR. ORIE: Professor Hayden ---- 4 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: I am sorry.
